Prior to the emergence of incretin-based therapies, no pharmacologic agent held approval for nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) or its progressive form, nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), leaving weight loss through lifestyle modification as the sole recommended intervention despite its well-documented difficulty to sustain [@Khan2026Therapeutic]. That landscape has shifted: semaglutide, a single-target glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA), now stands alongside resmetirom as one of only two agents to have received accelerated regulatory approval for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), reflecting a body of placebo-controlled trial evidence that has matured enough to inform treatment guidelines [@Chan2026Pharmacological].

The most rigorous synthesis of this evidence comes from a systematic review and meta-analysis of placebo-controlled randomized trials of subcutaneous semaglutide in NAFLD/NASH, which applied Cochrane RoB 2 risk-of-bias assessment and GRADE certainty rating [@Khan2026Therapeutic]. Semaglutide significantly reduced aspartate aminotransferase (mean difference [MD] -6.72 U/L; 95% CI -11.79 to -1.64; P = .009) and more than doubled the odds of NASH resolution without fibrosis progression (RR 2.14; 95% CI 1.44-3.17; P = .0002). Fibrosis-stage improvement, by contrast, favored semaglutide numerically but did not reach significance (RR 1.14; 95% CI 0.63-2.05; P = .67). Weight loss (MD -6.99%; 95% CI -13.92 to -0.06; P = .05) and glycated hemoglobin reduction (MD -1.29%; 95% CI -1.46 to -1.13; P < .00001) were the co-primary metabolic drivers underlying these hepatic effects, with gastrointestinal adverse events and discontinuation more common on active drug but serious adverse events comparable to placebo. An independent, updated meta-analysis of ten trials (n = 1908; PROSPERO CRD420261288562) corroborated this pattern: semaglutide markedly improved MASH resolution without worsening fibrosis (OR 3.48; 95% CI 2.68-4.53; P < .00001), reduced liver stiffness (MD -1.25 kPa; 95% CI -2.18 to -0.32; P = .009), and increased the odds of a ≥30% relative reduction in liver fat content (OR 7.16; 95% CI 3.08-16.64; P < .00001), while pooled fibrosis improvement of at least one stage again fell short of significance (OR 1.17; 95% CI 0.49-2.80; P = .72) [@Peng2026Clinical]. Across both syntheses, the anti-steatotic and anti-inflammatory signal is robust; the anti-fibrotic signal is directionally favorable but statistically fragile.

This histologic profile is consistent with the individual trials underpinning it. In the liraglutide LEAN trial, steatohepatitis resolution without fibrosis worsening occurred in 39% of treated patients versus 9% on placebo; semaglutide's phase 2 dose-ranging trial showed dose-dependent resolution rates up to 59% versus 17% with placebo; and in a subsequent trial of semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly, an interim analysis in patients with F2-F3 MASH met both co-primary histologic endpoints, with resolution without fibrosis worsening in 62.9% versus 34.3% and fibrosis improvement of at least one stage in 36.8% versus 22.4% of placebo-treated patients [@Amorim2026GLP]. A systematic review spanning twelve studies of GLP-1RA monotherapy similarly found hepatic fat reduction to be the most consistent finding across agents, demonstrated with semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, and beinaglutide, while liver-enzyme improvement was less uniform and best regarded as supportive rather than definitive; histologic benefit was strongest for steatohepatitis resolution in non-cirrhotic MASH, and fibrosis benefit clustered in F2-F3 disease with limited response once cirrhosis was established [@Mahoon2026Therapeutic]. A broader meta-analysis of 24 randomized trials (n = 2158) comparing incretin therapies with placebo, oral hypoglycemics, or insulin found consistent reductions in ALT (SMD -0.46 vs placebo; -1.02 vs insulin), AST (SMD -0.41 vs placebo; -0.62 vs insulin), and liver fat (SMD -0.62 vs insulin), with steatohepatitis resolution greater than placebo but not clearly superior to insulin, and benefits generally larger among patients with coexisting diabetes — underscoring glycemic and weight-related mechanisms as shared drivers of hepatic response [@Tesoro2026Impact].

Substantial heterogeneity nonetheless runs through this literature. An umbrella review of 23 meta-analyses applying AMSTAR 2 found that outcomes clustered into five domains — liver characteristics, enzyme levels, anthropometrics, metabolic markers, and inflammatory markers — but nearly 80% of the included reviews were of critically low methodological quality with substantial evidence overlap, leading the authors to characterize the pooled evidence base as preliminary and hypothesis-generating rather than conclusive [@Wu2026Efficacy]. Differences in population severity, treatment duration, and outcome definitions compound this uncertainty: a conceptual analysis proposing a multi-layered regulatory framework for GLP-1RA action specifically flags advanced fibrosis, metabolically milder populations, and treatment discontinuation as recurring settings of limited therapeutic response, suggesting that indirect, systemic mechanisms of hepatic benefit may saturate once intrahepatic or systemic signaling capacity is exhausted [@Zhou2026From]. Even the definition of the population meant to benefit is unsettled; work applying magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) in 413 biopsied patients showed that a simplified at-risk MASH definition (fibrosis stage ≥2) captured substantially more treatment candidates than a stricter NAFLD Activity Score-based definition (122 vs 77 patients), and that optimized liver-stiffness cutoffs (2.8-6.4 kPa) identified 28% more biopsy-proven pharmacotherapy candidates than AASLD-recommended thresholds, improving sensitivity from 50% to 80% — a reminder that eligibility criteria alone can materially shift apparent trial effect sizes [@Li2026Simplified].

The advanced fibrosis and compensated cirrhosis population remains the starkest evidence gap. Few placebo-controlled trials enroll patients with F4 compensated cirrhosis (F4c), but a phase 2, dose-ranging trial that included this population is instructive: among 698 randomized participants, semaglutide 2.4 mg monotherapy achieved fibrosis improvement with no MASH worsening at week 52 in 30% of patients versus 16% on placebo, a nominally significant difference (estimated difference in responder proportions 14.05; 95% CI 1.88-26.23; P = .024), even though combining semaglutide with the investigational agent zalfermin did not significantly outperform placebo (24% vs 16%; P = .19) [@Loomba2026Efficacy]. This trial offers rare direct evidence that semaglutide monotherapy retains an anti-fibrotic signal even in a cirrhosis-inclusive population, though the effect size is modest and the trial was not powered for this comparison alone.

Real-world comparative evidence against sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) is similarly mixed rather than uniformly favorable to GLP-1RAs. A propensity-matched TriNetX cohort of over 180,000 patients found semaglutide initiators had markedly lower one-year hazards of mortality (HR 0.38), hospitalization (HR 0.44), major cardiovascular events (HR 0.50), and major adverse liver outcomes (HR 0.36) compared with SGLT2i initiators, with attenuated but still favorable hazard ratios at five years [@Khalil2026Efficacy], and a genotype-stratified propensity-matched study similarly found subcutaneous GLP-1RA superior to SGLT2i for HbA1c and BMI reduction and the only class producing significant ALT reduction in the MASLD subgroup (P = .02) [@Toffoli2026Comparative]. Yet a separate propensity-matched cohort of 705 patients with type 2 diabetes and NAFLD reported the opposite direction for liver enzymes, with SGLT2i producing significantly greater ALT and AST reductions than GLP-1RAs at six months (P = .011 and P = .010, respectively) [@Guo2026Effects], and an exploratory meta-analysis of real-world comparative cohorts versus DPP-4 inhibitors found only a modest, very-low-certainty signal for reduced incident cirrhosis or composite serious liver events (HR 0.85; 95% CI 0.74-0.98) [@Hu2026Glucagonlike]. Beyond the liver-specific comparisons, liraglutide 3.0 mg initiated early after bariatric surgery produced dose-dependent total weight loss (16.3% at six months vs 5.3% with standard care; P < .05) alongside remission of MASLD and hyperuricemia, reinforcing weight loss magnitude as a proximate mediator of hepatic benefit independent of the specific comparator [@Ouyang2026Optimal].

Taken together, the totality of placebo-controlled and comparative evidence supports GLP-1RA monotherapy, and semaglutide specifically, as an effective intervention for steatosis regression, biochemical improvement, and steatohepatitis resolution in non-cirrhotic MASLD/MASH, with weight loss and glycemic control as the principal mediating drivers. The fibrosis and advanced-disease evidence base is comparatively thin: pooled fibrosis-stage improvement remains statistically inconsistent, GRADE-rated certainty is generally low to very low for hard liver outcomes, and only limited trial data — largely from a single phase 2 study — directly address compensated cirrhosis. This asymmetry between strong steatohepatitis-resolution evidence and fragile fibrosis evidence is precisely what current guideline updates must reconcile as GLP-1RAs move from adjunctive metabolic therapy toward a foundational role in MASLD pharmacotherapy.
